title: The Akathist
hookLine: a Byzantine hymn to Mary sung standing

lines: A HYMN NAMED FOR NOT SITTING.
THE PEOPLE STAY ON THEIR FEET.
cards: Here's a hymn whose name is an instruction about chairs. In the Byzantine churches, the Orthodox and the Eastern Catholic churches, there's a long hymn to Mary that nobody sits down for.
Its name, the Akathist, means not sitting. The church fills, the singing starts, and the people stay on their feet, stanza after stanza, while one greeting comes around again and again: rejoice.
A story people tell says it was once sung through a whole night, standing, by a city giving thanks for being saved from a siege. Whatever its history, the posture stuck.

teach.b: Akathistos, in Greek, means not seated. Standing is what a person does when someone they honor walks into the room, and the hymn makes that a whole service: the body says what the words are saying.
Some people stand to show respect; some stand because they can't sit still with joy. This hymn asks for both. Then the greeting.
The word that keeps returning is chaire, rejoice, or hail. It's the angel's word. In Luke's Gospel, Gabriel opens with it, which the Douay-Rheims renders "Hail, full of grace, the Lord is with thee."
The Akathist multiplies that one greeting, line after line, each rejoice hung with a new picture of Mary, the way the Litany of Loreto stacks its names.
At the end of each long stanza comes the refrain: rejoice, unwedded bride.
Then the story underneath. The hymn doesn't only praise; it walks through the Gospel. Gabriel's visit.
The birth. The shepherds. The magi following the star.

The rejoices rise out of the story, like applause at each turn of a play. Last, where it lives. Eastern churches sing it especially in Lent, and that includes the Byzantine Catholic churches, in full communion with Rome.
For a Latin Catholic, it's a reminder that the Church breathes, in a phrase Pope John Paul the Second used, with two lungs, East and West.
The same Mary, the same angel's word, said in a different key, and on your feet.

how: Orthodox and Eastern Catholic Christians sing the Akathist to the Mother of God standing, especially in Lent, and some pray it at home or in shorter parts through the week.

games.q: the hymn to Mary begins, and it's going to be long. what does the congregation do?
o: stand for the whole of it.
games.why: they stand. the hymn's very name, akathistos, means not seated.

practice: If you're able, stand up now; if you can't, sit up tall and let that be your standing, feet steady, shoulders loose, the way you'd straighten if someone had just walked in.
If you pray, say the angel's greeting, hail, full of grace, the Lord is with thee, or the refrain, rejoice, unwedded bride, once with each slow breath.
If you don't, simply stand in honor of someone you love, and let your body say it.
